claims.text: You are about to explore the Palais Lascaris in Nice, home to a remarkable collection of ancient musical instruments.
Encounter the exquisite craftsmanship of the Harpe by Naderman, Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer, Violes gambe by William Turner, and Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore.
Discover the rediscovered Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780) and the distinctive maker's mark on the Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer (Nuremberg, 1581) as you journey through this musical tour.
Your first stop is Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780).
Stand before the Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780) at the Palais Lascaris in Nice and let your eyes wander over the intricate carvings and gilded embellishments.
In 1780, Jean-Henri Naderman, a renowned luthier based in Paris, crafted the harp before you.
claims.evidence: The harp was built in Paris in 1780 by Jean-Henri Naderman, a Westphalia-born luthier active in Paris from roughly the mid-18th century until his death in 1799.

claims.text: This innovation enabled more complex compositions and nuanced performances, cementing his reputation in the realm of French musical instruments.
The harp was initially owned by the Viscountess of Beaumont, integrating it into the elegant social circles of 18th-century France.
In 1995, the harp was rediscovered in the attic of the Château de Busset in France, long after it had fallen into obscurity.
claims.evidence: The harp was rediscovered in 1995 stored in the attic of the Château de Busset in the Allier department of France.

claims.text: Its revival led to the City of Nice acquiring it in 2007, ensuring its preservation and subsequent display at the Musée du Palais Lascaris.
This acquisition placed the harp among the second most significant collection of musical instruments in France, right after the Musée de la Musique de la Philharmonie in Paris.

Now housed among over 500 instruments, the Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780) stands as an emblem of both artistic beauty and technological advancement at a time when the French court reveled in opulence.
Stand before the Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer, crafted in Nuremberg in 1581.
In the late 16th century, Anton Schnitzer, a master craftsman from Nuremberg, produced this tenor sackbut, known today as one of the earliest surviving examples of its kind in original condition.
Schnitzer's distinct maker's mark and the year of production, 1581, are inscribed on the bell rim, bearing testimony to his expertise in brass instrument making.
In 2001, the sackbut found a new home at the Palais Lascaris, a venue dedicated to celebrating the history of musical instruments.
Its presence here offers a tangible link to the period when brass instruments like the sackbut bridged medieval music with the Renaissance tide, paving the way for modern trombones.
As you approach William Turner's viola da gamba, crafted in London in 1652, notice how the light catches its original carved head and pegbox, reflecting its nearly untouched state over the centuries.
In 1652, the English luthier William Turner crafted a six-string bass viola da gamba in his workshop located near Aldgate.
claims.evidence: The instrument was made in 1652 in London by the English luthier William Turner, who was active in the mid-17th century and had a workshop located in Gravel Lane near Aldgate.

claims.text: Antoine Gautier, a dedicated Niçois amateur musician and avid collector, bequeathed the viol to the public collections of Nice, the city where he was born, in 1904, allowing it to become a cherished part of the Palais Lascaris.
Now imagine what innovation came next — the viols and violins crafted by Italian artisans known for their unparalleled craftsmanship.
